outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — China has denied entry to Hong Kong for nine U.S. Navy ships and one Air Force jet over the past month, U.S. military officials said Friday.

China refused the USS Reuben James, a Navy frigate shown in a 1989 photo, permission to make a Christmas port call in Hong Kong. Senior Navy officials said Beijing denied the ship’s request for a holiday visit for sailors at the end of December.

The rejection occurred last week, at the same time China refused to allow the USS Kitty Hawk aircraft carrier battle group to enter Hong Kong for a Thanksgiving holiday port call. A U.S. Air Force C-17 flight scheduled for a routine resupply of the U.S. Consulate in Hong Kong was also denied permission to enter, Navy officials said.

The Kitty Hawk battle group was eventually granted permission to enter, but by then the ships were already well on their way to port in Japan. Days earlier, China had refused to grant two U.S. Navy minesweepers safe harbor in Hong Kong during a storm on the high seas.

The United States has filed a formal protest with China over the decisions.

U.S. officials said they remain baffled by the reason, or reasons, behind the port-call refusals. China has recently expressed concern over U.S. arms sales to Taiwan and President Bush’s October presentation of a Congressional Gold Medal to the Dalai Lama, the exiled Tibetan spiritual leader.

There is speculation that the Chinese may have been conducting military exercises they did not want the U.S. Navy to observe. Others believe the refusals may have resulted from a misunderstanding.

Officials could not explain why the rejection of the Reuben James had not been disclosed earlier, even though reporters had repeatedly asked whether there were any other pending port calls. One senior Navy official expressed dismay that the information had not been made public by the Pentagon.

White House deputy spokesman Scott Stanzel told reporters that the White House is “aware” of the latest refusals and referred questions to the Pentagon. Stanzel said Washington was seeking “clarification” from Beijing on the matter.

White House and other Bush administration officials have sought to defuse tensions with China, saying the United States wants to move forward on broader issues of military cooperation.

Meanwhile, Navy officials say Japan is tightening approvals for Chinese navy visits to its ports. Crew members from a Chinese ship making a port call in Japan may not be allowed to tour a Japanese Aegis warship.

The U.S.-designed Aegis weapons system enables coordinated operations against threats from aircraft and missiles, surface ships, and submarines. It is not clear whether the Japanese decision was made at the request of the United States.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — U.S. military officials said Friday that, over the previous month, China had blocked nine U.S. Navy vessels and one Air Force aircraft from entering Hong Kong.

Among the ships turned away was the USS Reuben James, a Navy frigate shown in a 1989 photograph, which China denied permission to visit Hong Kong for a Christmas port stop. Senior Navy officials said Beijing rejected the request for the Reuben James to make a late-December holiday visit so its sailors could spend time ashore.

That refusal took place the previous week, around the same time China also barred the USS Kitty Hawk aircraft carrier battle group from entering Hong Kong for a Thanksgiving port visit. Navy officials said permission was also denied for a U.S. Air Force C-17 flight that had been planned as a routine resupply mission for the U.S. Consulate in Hong Kong.

China later reversed course and approved the Kitty Hawk group’s entry, but by that point the ships were already far along on their route to a port in Japan. A few days before that, Beijing had also refused to allow two U.S. Navy minesweepers to take shelter in Hong Kong while they were facing a storm at sea.

The United States has submitted a formal diplomatic protest to China over the refusals. U.S. officials said they were puzzled about why the port calls had been rejected.

China has recently voiced objections to U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, as well as to President Bush’s October decision to present the Congressional Gold Medal to the Dalai Lama, Tibet’s exiled spiritual leader.

There has also been speculation that China may have been carrying out military drills it did not want the U.S. Navy to observe. Others have suggested the denials could have stemmed from a misunderstanding.

Officials were unable to explain why the refusal involving the Reuben James had not previously been revealed, despite reporters repeatedly asking whether any other port visits were awaiting approval. One senior Navy official said he was troubled that the Pentagon had not released the information earlier.

White House deputy spokesman Scott Stanzel told journalists that the White House was “aware” of the newest refusals and directed further questions to the Pentagon. He said Washington was seeking a “clarification” from Beijing.

Officials at the White House and elsewhere in the Bush administration have tried to ease friction with China, saying the United States wants to continue working with Beijing on wider military cooperation.

At the same time, Navy officials said Japan is becoming more restrictive in approving Chinese naval visits to Japanese ports. Crew members from a Chinese ship visiting Japan may be barred from touring a Japanese Aegis warship.

The Aegis weapons system, designed in the United States, allows coordinated defense operations against aircraft and missile threats, surface vessels, and submarines. It was not clear whether Japan’s decision had been made at the request of the United States.

The dispute underscored how quickly routine military arrangements can become entangled in broader strategic tensions. **U.S.-China tensions rise after Beijing denies Hong Kong port calls to American military vessels**

*By Staff Reporter*

Tensions between the United States and China have escalated after Beijing denied requests for U.S. military vessels and a support aircraft to make scheduled stops in Hong Kong, U.S. officials said.

The Pentagon said China refused permission for two planned port visits by American military assets, including a U.S. Navy ship and a resupply aircraft, amid heightened political friction over Hong Kong and broader disputes between Washington and Beijing.

U.S. defense officials described the denials as “unhelpful” and said the United States has a long history of conducting routine port calls in Hong Kong. Such visits are typically used for rest, resupply and logistical support, and are generally arranged through diplomatic channels.

China did not immediately provide a detailed explanation for the decision, but the move comes during a period of strained relations between the two countries. Disagreements over trade, technology, Taiwan, the South China Sea and U.S. criticism of Beijing’s handling of Hong Kong have all contributed to a sharp deterioration in ties.

Hong Kong has long served as a frequent stop for U.S. Navy vessels operating in the Indo-Pacific region. However, Beijing has previously suspended or denied American military visits to the city during periods of diplomatic tension, using access to Hong Kong ports as a signal of displeasure with U.S. policy.

The latest refusal follows repeated U.S. statements expressing concern about political freedoms and civil liberties in Hong Kong. Chinese officials have accused Washington of interfering in China’s internal affairs, particularly over U.S. support for pro-democracy activists and criticism of Beijing’s tightening control over the territory.

The United States maintains that its naval operations in the region are routine and lawful. U.S. officials said the denied visits would not affect the military’s ability to operate in the Indo-Pacific, where American forces continue to conduct patrols, exercises and freedom-of-navigation operations.

Analysts say the denial is largely symbolic but underscores the fragile state of U.S.-China relations.

“Port calls are not usually a central issue in military strategy, but they carry diplomatic weight,” said one regional security analyst. “When Beijing blocks them, it is often intended as a political message to Washington.”

The incident adds to a growing list of disputes between the world’s two largest economies. Despite periodic diplomatic engagement, both governments remain at odds over military activity near China’s coast, export controls, sanctions, cybersecurity and competing influence across Asia.

U.S. officials said they would continue to seek communication with Chinese counterparts to reduce the risk of miscalculation. But with both countries taking increasingly firm positions, the denial of port access in Hong Kong is likely to be viewed in Washington as another sign of deepening rivalry.

**U.S. officials: China refused entry to nine Navy ships and an Air Force C-17 in Hong Kong**

**Washington** — China refused port calls or landing requests in Hong Kong for nine U.S. Navy ships and one U.S. Air Force C-17 transport aircraft over the past month, U.S. officials said, a move that appeared to underscore rising tensions between Washington and Beijing.

The denials affected routine U.S. military requests to stop in Hong Kong, long a favored port of call for American sailors in the Pacific. The officials said the rejected requests included visits by multiple Navy vessels and a C-17 aircraft that had sought to land in Hong Kong.

U.S. officials did not immediately provide a full public list of the ships involved or specify the operational reasons for each request. They described the denials as unusual in volume, though China has previously restricted or canceled U.S. military visits to Hong Kong during periods of diplomatic strain.

Hong Kong, a semi-autonomous Chinese territory, has historically served as a major rest stop for U.S. Navy crews operating in the region. Port visits there allow sailors time ashore and give U.S. vessels an opportunity for maintenance, logistics and resupply. While all such visits require Chinese approval, denials have often been seen in Washington as a political signal from Beijing.

The latest refusals come against the backdrop of continuing friction between the United States and China over military activity in the South China Sea, Taiwan, trade disputes, human rights issues and U.S. alliances in the Indo-Pacific.

China has repeatedly objected to U.S. military operations near areas claimed by Beijing, including freedom-of-navigation operations conducted by the U.S. Navy. Washington says those missions are meant to uphold international law and preserve access to international waters and airspace. Beijing has accused the U.S. of militarizing the region and threatening Chinese sovereignty.

A U.S. defense official said the denials would not prevent the U.S. military from operating in the Indo-Pacific, where American forces maintain a large and permanent presence through bases, rotational deployments and allied partnerships.

“We continue to fly, sail and operate wherever international law allows,” the official said.

The Chinese government did not immediately comment on the latest U.S. claims. In past cases, Beijing has said decisions on Hong Kong port calls are handled “case by case” and depend on the broader state of U.S.-China relations.

The refusals also highlight Hong Kong’s diminishing role as a neutral stopover point for U.S. forces amid Beijing’s tightening control over the city. Since the 2020 imposition of a national security law, the U.S. has said Hong Kong no longer enjoys the same level of autonomy it was promised under the “one country, two systems” framework.

For decades, U.S. military visits to Hong Kong were a visible symbol of pragmatic cooperation between the two countries, even during tense periods. Sailors on liberty in the city were once a common sight, and port calls brought economic benefits to local businesses.

But military access has become increasingly vulnerable to political disputes. China has previously denied U.S. port visits following American arms sales to Taiwan or other moves Beijing viewed as provocative.

Analysts say the latest cluster of denials could be intended as a warning to Washington at a time when the U.S. is strengthening military ties with allies and partners across the region, including Japan, the Philippines and Australia.

The Pentagon has emphasized that it is building a more distributed force posture in the Pacific to reduce reliance on any single location. Still, the loss of Hong Kong as a dependable port option complicates planning for ships operating in the western Pacific.

The U.S. State Department and Pentagon are expected to raise the matter through diplomatic and military channels, officials said. But there was no immediate indication that the denials had triggered a broader change in U.S. operations.
